questions.question: What is the primary reason the lecturer recommends using assumptions instead of breaking problems into sub-problems?
questions.gold_answer: Breaking problems into sub-problems can become overly mathematical and difficult to understand, whereas making assumptions leverages our natural human tendency to make judgments.
questions.quote: Most people learn to solve DP problems by breaking them into sub-problems. And when you try to do that, the approach becomes quite mathematical and hard to understand. That's why, instead of thinking in terms of sub-problems, I recommend making an assumption.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the recursive rule in the context of the longest-increasing subsequence problem?
questions.gold_answer: The recursive rule formalizes the logic of checking all previous indices to see if a current number can extend an existing subsequence to create a longer one.
questions.quote: Recursive rule is just a fancy way of formalizing what we have already discussed. To find the length of the longest-increasing subsequence ending at the current last index, we go through all the indices to the left of it.

questions.question: How does the lecturer define the base case for the longest-increasing subsequence problem?
questions.gold_answer: The base case is defined by initializing the length of the longest-increasing subsequence ending at any index to 1, because each individual number is a subsequence of length 1.
questions.quote: Each number by itself can be seen as a subsequence of length 1, ending at its own index. And this subsequence is an increasing subsequence because it has only one number. So the initial length for the longest-increasing subsequence ending at any index would be 1.
